Lasso Regression with Boruta Feature Selection for Quantifying Coffee Adulteration: Spectral Preprocessing Using MSC, Savitzky-Golay, and First Derivative

Author

Derick Malavi

Introduction

Coffee adulteration, such as blending premium Arabica with lower-cost Robusta, undermines quality and authenticity, posing significant challenges for consumers, producers, and regulators. High-dimensional spectroscopic data provides valuable insights for detecting such fraud, but the large number of variables necessitates effective feature selection techniques to isolate the most relevant wavelengths.

This study incorporates the Boruta algorithm, a robust feature selection method that identifies relevant variables by iteratively comparing the importance of original features with randomized counterparts using a Random Forest framework. Boruta ensures the inclusion of critical spectral features while avoiding irrelevant or redundant variables, improving model interpretability and performance. Additionally, LASSO regression is employed as a feature selection and prediction method, shrinking irrelevant feature coefficients to zero and effectively handling multicollinearity while reducing the dataset’s dimensionality.

The study aims to use LASSO regression to predict Arabica coffee adulterated with Robusta at levels ranging from 1% to 80%, leveraging advanced feature selection and regression techniques to enhance model accuracy and robustness.

Prepare Data

# Load data: msc_sg_1d spectra

hsi_msc_sg_1d <- read.csv("coffee_ground_msc_sg_1d.csv")

# Ensure we have the same number of dimensions and the range of our columns/covariates
dim(hsi_msc_sg_1d)
[1] 1469  229
# Check a few column names
col_check <- colnames(hsi_msc_sg_1d[,c(1:6)])
col_check
[1] "sample_id"     "binary_class"  "three_class"   "adult_percent"
[5] "cal_val"       "X935.609985"  
# our response variable (adulteration percentage) is column 4
# The spectral values start from column # 6 -------> 229

# Convert the adulteration percentage to numeric for compatibility with ML
hsi_msc_sg_1d$adult_percent <- as.numeric(hsi_msc_sg_1d$adult_percent)

Get the X and y variables

X <- hsi_msc_sg_1d[,c(6:229)]

Split the Data (Train_Test Split)

  • We want to select features based on training data only to avoid any data leakage that could inflate model performance and make the model less generalizable to unseen data.
# Subset samples for cross-validation and external validation (70/30)
# Record 1 under cal_val variable is for calibration while 2 will be for testing the model

sample<-hsi_msc_sg_1d$cal_val == 1 

# Split to train and test sets
X_train <- X[sample,]
X_test <- X[!sample,]
y_train <-y[sample]
y_test <- y[!sample]

# Check length of the subsets for training and validation
dim(X_train)
[1] 1055  224
dim(X_test)
[1] 414 224
length(y_train)
[1] 1055
length(y_test)
[1] 414
# Merge the test and train data
train_data <- data.frame(X_train, y_train)
test_data <- data.frame(X_test, y_test)

Run Boruta Algorithm for Optimum Wavelength Selection

  # Set seed for reproducibility 
  set.seed(123)

  # Set the dataset name dynamically
  dataset_name <- "msc_sg_1d"  

  # Define paths for the execution flag and Boruta result
  flag_file <- paste0("boruta_executed_flag_", dataset_name, ".RData")
  result_file <- paste0("boruta_result_", dataset_name, ".RData")

  # Register cluster for caret to train the models in parallel
  cl <- makeCluster(6, type = "SOCK")
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(registerDoSNOW(cl)))

if (!file.exists(result_file)) {
  message(paste("Starting Boruta execution for dataset:", dataset_name))
  
  # Start the timer
  start_time <- Sys.time()

  # Run Boruta on the train data set
  boruta_result <- Boruta(formula = y_train ~ .,  
                        data = train_data, 
                        doTrace = 2,
                        maxRuns = 100)                   
 
  # Stop the cluster
  stopCluster(cl)

  # Register end time
  end_time <- Sys.time()
  print(paste('Time to run the Boruta model:', end_time - start_time))  
  
  # Save Boruta results and execution flag
  boruta_executed <- TRUE
  save(boruta_executed, file = flag_file)
  save(boruta_result, file = result_file)
 

  message(paste("Boruta execution completed for dataset:", dataset_name, "and results saved."))

} else {
  # Load previously saved results
  message(paste("Result file found. Loading saved Boruta results for dataset:", dataset_name))
  load(result_file)
  load(flag_file)
  message(paste("Boruta already executed for dataset:", dataset_name))
}

Create a Data frame with the Selected Features

# Subset the training and test data using the selected features
X_train_selected <- X_train[, final_features]  
X_test_selected <- X_test[, final_features]   

# Keep y_train and y_test as-is 
y_train_selected <- y_train
y_test_selected <- y_test


#Merge data_frame
train_merged <- cbind(X_train_selected, y_train = y_train_selected)
test_merged <- cbind(X_test_selected, y_test = y_test_selected)

dim(train_merged)

Check correlations by HeatMaps

n_features <- length(final_features)

#Calculate correlations
corr <- cor(train_merged[, -(n_features+1)])

par(cex.main = 0.6)

Train Models

  • We will train models based on the reduced number of features.
# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed (123) 

# Set up the training control(10 folds 10 times cross_validation)
control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 10, 
                        savePredictions = "final", 
                        summaryFunction = defaultSummary,
                        selectionFunction = 'best', allowParallel = TRUE)

# We used oneSE for classification. For regression, we will use 'best': a model that minimizes RMSECV
#Set the metric as accuracy 
metric<-"RMSE"
# Hyperparameter set
# alpha: Set to 1 for LASSO (pure L1 regularization).
# lambda: Regularization strength (penalty parameter). A sequence of values is tested to identify the best lambda.

grid <- expand.grid(
  alpha = 1,   # LASSO (alpha = 1)
  lambda = seq(0.001, 0.1, length = 10)  
)

Train Lasso

set.seed(123)
#Register cluster for caret to train the models in parallel
cl<-makeCluster(6,type = "SOCK")
suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  registerDoSNOW(cl)))

# Start_time
start_time<-Sys.time()

#Train the model using cross-validation (10 folds, 10 times)
fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d<-train(y = train_merged[,(n_features+1)], 
                         x = train_merged[,-(n_features+1)],
                         method = 'glmnet', tuneGrid = grid,
                         trControl = control, preProcess = c("center","scale"),
                         metric = metric) 
#End_time
end_time<-Sys.time()

model_training_time<-end_time-start_time

stopCluster(cl) # Stop the parallel run cluster

print(model_training_time)
Time difference of 20.24712 secs

Best hyperparameters

# Best lambda value

cat("Best Lambda:", best_lambda, "\n")
Best Lambda: 0.001

Extract Selected Features

# Extract coefficients from the best model
coefficients <- coef(fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d$finalModel, s = best_lambda)

# Convert to a readable format
lasso_coefficients <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(coefficients))
colnames(lasso_coefficients) <- "Coefficient"
lasso_coefficients$Variable <- rownames(lasso_coefficients)

# Filter non-zero coefficients (selected features)
selected_features <- lasso_coefficients[lasso_coefficients$Coefficient != 0, ]
print(selected_features)

Save the models for future use

saveRDS(fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d, "fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d.rds")

Plot the cross-validation results —–> Model Selection

# Extract results and best lambda
lasso_data <- fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d$results
best_lambda <- fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d$bestTune$lambda
y_RMSE <- lasso_data$RMSE[lasso_data$lambda == best_lambda]

# Plot RMSE against lambda
plot(
  lasso_data$lambda, lasso_data$RMSE, type = "b", col = "black", pch = 8, cex.axis = 0.8,
  xlab = "Lambda", ylab = "RMSECV(%)", cex.lab = 0.9,
  main = "LASSO Optimal Model Selection", cex.main = 0.9, cex.lab = 0.8
)

# Add line from x-axis to the specific point (optimal lambda)
segments(x0 = best_lambda, y0 = 0, x1 = best_lambda, y1 = y_RMSE, col = "red", lty = 2)

# Add line from y-axis to the specific point (corresponding RMSE)
segments(x0 = 0, y0 = y_RMSE, x1 = best_lambda, y1 = y_RMSE, col = "red", lty = 2)

# Add annotation for the optimal point
text(best_lambda, y_RMSE, labels = paste0("(", round(best_lambda, 4), ", ", round(y_RMSE, 2), ")"), 
     pos = 3, col = "blue", cex = 0.8)

Coefficients vs. Lambda Path

# Extract the final glmnet model 
fit_glmnet <- fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d$finalModel

# Plot coefficients vs. lambda
plot(
  fit_glmnet, 
  xvar = "lambda",      
  label = FALSE,         
  cex.axis = 0.8,       
  cex.lab = 0.9,        
  cex.main = 0.3)
title(main = "Coefficient Path for LASSO Regression")
#As lambda increases, coefficients shrink toward zero, highlighting the feature selection process

Test the model performance on test data

#Predict on the test set 
observed <- test_merged$y_test
predictions <- predict(fit_lasso_msc_sg_1d,newdata=test_merged)

# Generate predictions
results <- postResample(predictions, observed)

print(results)
     RMSE  Rsquared       MAE 
9.4157524 0.9092786 7.7405575 
RMSEP = results[[1]]
R2 = results[[2]]
MAE = results[[3]]

cat('The RMSEP for the model on external validation is:', RMSEP,'\n')
The RMSEP for the model on external validation is: 9.415752 
cat('The R Squared value for the model is:', R2)
The R Squared value for the model is: 0.9092786
# Calculate Residual Predictive Deviation to check model performance

RPD = sd(observed)/RMSEP

print(paste('The RPD values for the model is', round(RPD,2)))
[1] "The RPD values for the model is 3.09"

Visualizations

# predicted vs observed line and scatter
# Create a data frame
results_df <- data.frame(observed=observed, predictions=predictions)

results_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = observed, y = predictions)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", 
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs( x = "Measured Adulteration (%)",
    y = "Predicted Adulteration (%)") +
  annotate("text",
    x = min(observed), y = max(predictions),
    label = paste("RMSEP:", round(RMSEP, 2),
      "\nR-squared:", round(R2, 3),
      "\nRPD:", round(RPD, 2)),
    hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3, color = "black") +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(color = "black", size = 10),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))+
  theme_gray()
# Check residuals

residuals <- observed - predictions

# Plot Residuals
plot(predictions, residuals,
     xlab = "Predicted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Predicted",
     pch = 16, col = "blue")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)  
hist(residuals, 
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals", cex.main = 0.8,
     col = "lightblue", border = "black"); box()

Conclusion

  • Boruta algorithm and lasso demonstrate excellent performance in predicting adulteration in ground coffee. The model achieves an RPD value of 3.1. The model is highly accurate and reliable for analytical and quantitative applications.
